title: Salk, Sabin and the Polio Pioneers
summary: Jonas Salk made a polio vaccine from killed virus, and almost two million children helped test it in the biggest medical trial the world had ever seen. Then Albert Sabin made a different vaccine you could swallow on a sugar cube. Together their vaccines made polio cases crash, and today the disease is close to being gone for good.

sections.heading: Jonas Salk's Killed-Virus Plan
paragraphs: Jonas Salk was born in New York City on 28 October 1914, the son of Jewish immigrant parents who had little money but big hopes for their children. He was the first in his family to go to university, studying chemistry at the City College of New York and then medicine at New York University. Instead of treating patients one at a time, he decided he wanted to do research that could help millions of people at once.

In 1941 he went to the University of Michigan to work with the virologist Thomas Francis Jr., one of America's leading experts on influenza. Together they worked on a flu vaccine for the US Army during the Second World War. That vaccine used influenza virus that had been killed with chemicals, and it worked. The experience convinced Salk of something important: you did not need a live virus to teach the immune system. A killed, or inactivated, virus could still show the body the virus's shape, its antigens, so the body could make antibodies against it.

In 1947 Salk set up his own laboratory at the University of Pittsburgh. The next year, the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, the March of Dimes charity you met in the last part, asked him to join a huge, dull but essential project: sorting all the known samples of poliovirus into types. The work confirmed that there were exactly three types of poliovirus. That mattered enormously. Any vaccine would have to protect against all three, or children would still catch the types it missed.

Salk then set to work on his vaccine. His team grew large amounts of each of the three types of poliovirus in flasks of monkey kidney cells, using the tissue culture method that John Enders, Thomas Weller and Frederick Robbins had pioneered. They then treated the virus with formaldehyde, a chemical that damages the virus so it can no longer infect cells, while leaving its outer shape mostly intact. The trick was getting the dose and timing exactly right: too little formaldehyde and some virus might survive; too much and the virus might be so damaged that it no longer trained the immune system well. Salk worked out careful rules for how long to treat the virus, and tested every batch.

In 1952 he began testing his vaccine in people. On 2 July 1952 he vaccinated 43 children at the D.T. Watson Home for Crippled Children near Pittsburgh, many of whom already had antibodies because they had survived polio. A few weeks later he vaccinated children and adults at the Polk State School, a home for people with intellectual disabilities. Today we would ask hard questions about testing a new vaccine at such institutions, where people could not easily give their own free consent; in the 1950s, rules about medical research were far weaker than they are now. In 1953 Salk vaccinated himself, his wife and his three sons, to show how much he trusted his work. Blood tests showed that vaccinated people were making antibodies against poliovirus, and nobody became ill. It was promising, but promising is not proof. To know whether the vaccine actually prevented polio, it would need to be tested on a gigantic scale.

sections.heading: Henrietta's Cells
paragraphs: Testing a vaccine on hundreds of thousands of children meant doing an enormous number of laboratory tests: checking batches for live virus, and checking blood samples for antibodies. Those tests needed living cells, and monkey cells were expensive and limited. A surprising answer came from a hospital in Baltimore, and from a young woman who never knew about it.

Henrietta Lacks was an African American mother of five, born in 1920 in Virginia. In early 1951 she went to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, one of the few hospitals in the area that treated Black patients at the time, because she was ill. Doctors found she had cervical cancer. During her treatment, a surgeon took small samples of tissue from her tumour. Nobody asked her permission or told her what the samples would be used for. Sadly, the cancer spread quickly, and Henrietta Lacks died on 4 October 1951. She was 31 years old.

Her tissue samples went to the lab of a researcher named George Gey, who had been trying for years to keep human cells alive and dividing in the lab. Every earlier attempt had failed: human cells would divide a few times and then die. But Henrietta's cancer cells were different. They divided again and again, doubling roughly every day, and never stopped. Gey's lab named them HeLa cells, from the first two letters of her first and last names. They became the first human cells that could be grown in huge amounts indefinitely, which is why scientists call them an immortal cell line.

HeLa cells turned out to be easily infected by poliovirus, and when they were infected they died in a way scientists could see under a microscope. That made them perfect for polio testing. To supply the vaccine trial, a special laboratory was set up at the Tuskegee Institute, a historically Black university in Alabama, where a team of Black scientists and technicians grew HeLa cells in very large quantities and shipped them to testing labs around the country. HeLa cells went on to be used in research on cancer, viruses, genetics and many other areas, in labs all over the world.

Henrietta Lacks's family was not told about her cells until 1975, more than twenty years after her death, when they found out almost by chance. They were hurt and confused to learn that a part of her was being used all over the world while they had not even been asked. Her story became widely known through the 2010 book The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks by Rebecca Skloot. In 2013 the US National Institutes of Health reached an agreement giving her family a say in how the genetic information from HeLa cells is shared. In 2021 the World Health Organization gave a special award to her son Lawrence Lacks to honour her contribution to medicine.

Henrietta Lacks did not volunteer and did not donate her cells; they were taken without her knowledge. Today, rules in many countries require that people be told and asked before their tissue is used for research. Her story is now an important part of how scientists think about fairness, consent and respect, and it is a reminder that the polio vaccine, like so many advances, depended on people whose names were left out of the first history books.

sections.heading: The Polio Pioneers
paragraphs: In 1954 the National Foundation organised the biggest test of a medical product the world had ever seen. To make sure the results would be trusted, it asked Salk's old mentor Thomas Francis Jr. to run the trial independently from the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. Salk himself would not be in charge of judging his own vaccine. That separation was a key part of good science: the person who invented something should not be the only one deciding whether it works.

The trial began in late April 1954 in McLean, Virginia, and spread across 44 US states, as well as parts of Canada and Finland. In the end about 1.8 million children took part, most of them in their first, second or third year of primary school. They became known as the Polio Pioneers, and many received a little button or card to prove it. Parents had to sign forms agreeing to let their children take part, and hundreds of thousands of parents did, which shows how frightened they were of polio and how much they hoped for a vaccine.

Francis used two different designs at once. In some areas, children in the second grade were offered the vaccine, while children in the first and third grades were simply watched to see how many caught polio. These were called observed controls. In other areas, Francis used a stronger design, called a placebo-controlled, double-blind trial, in which some children received a placebo, a harmless injection that looked exactly the same but contained no vaccine. Across the whole trial, about 440,000 children received the real vaccine, about 210,000 received a placebo, and around 1.2 million more were observed controls.

Double-blind meant that neither the children and their parents nor the doctors and nurses giving the injections knew who was getting the real vaccine and who was getting the placebo. Each bottle had only a code number. Why go to such trouble? Because people's hopes and fears can influence what they see. If a doctor knew a child had been vaccinated, they might, without meaning to, be less likely to diagnose a mild case of polio as polio. Blinding protects the results from those hidden biases, so that any difference between the two groups is very likely to come from the vaccine itself.

The trial was a gigantic team effort. More than 100 staff at the University of Michigan worked on it, along with tens of thousands of doctors, nurses, school principals and teachers, plus a huge network of community volunteers who kept records and organised schedules. Each child needed three injections. Blood samples were collected from some children to measure antibodies. Every reported case of polio among the participants was carefully investigated. The records filled mountains of paper, and the results were counted with the help of punched-card tabulating machines, early ancestors of computers. The cost was about 17.5 million dollars, paid largely from the dimes and dollars of ordinary people. Then the whole country had to wait almost a year for the answer.

sections.heading: Safe, Effective and Potent
paragraphs: On the morning of 12 April 1955, hundreds of people crowded into the Rackham Auditorium at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. There were scientists, officials from the National Foundation, and a large crowd of reporters, with television cameras and radio microphones ready. Across the country, people gathered around radios and televisions, and some cities even arranged for the news to be broadcast in public. The date had been chosen with care: it was exactly ten years since the death of Franklin Roosevelt, the man who had started the March of Dimes.

Thomas Francis Jr. stepped up to report the results. In plain words, the message that went round the world was that the Salk vaccine was safe, effective and potent. In the placebo-controlled part of the trial, the vaccine was about 60 to 70 percent effective against type 1 poliovirus, the most common cause of paralysis, and over 90 percent effective against types 2 and 3. It was about 94 percent effective against bulbar polio, the deadly kind that stopped people breathing. It was not perfect, as no vaccine is, but it was a huge step forward.

The reaction was astonishing. Church bells rang in some towns. Shops put signs in their windows saying thank you, Dr Salk. Teachers let classes out early. That same afternoon, the US government licensed the vaccine, and companies that had already been making it in advance began shipping it out. Jonas Salk, who was 40 years old, became one of the most famous people in the world almost overnight.

That evening, the television journalist Edward R. Murrow interviewed Salk and asked him who owned the patent on the vaccine. Salk replied that it belonged to the people, and then asked, could you patent the sun? A patent is a legal right that lets an inventor control who can make an invention and charge money for it. Historians point out that lawyers had already looked into whether the vaccine could be patented and doubted it could, because it used methods that were already known. Even so, Salk's answer became famous, and he never made money from the vaccine itself.

Salk was careful to praise the many people who had helped, but some of his colleagues felt he had not mentioned their names enough in his speech that day, and some fellow scientists were jealous of his sudden fame. He later founded the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in La Jolla, California, which opened in 1963 and is still a leading research centre. He died in 1995, at the age of 80.

sections.heading: The Cutter Incident
paragraphs: Within days of the celebration, something went badly wrong. Several companies were making the Salk vaccine, and making it on a huge scale for the first time. One of them, Cutter Laboratories in Berkeley, California, produced some batches in which the formaldehyde had not killed all of the virus. Some of the vaccine still contained live, dangerous poliovirus.

In late April 1955, doctors began reporting cases of paralytic polio in children who had just received the vaccine, often starting in the arm where they had been injected. On 27 April Cutter's vaccine was withdrawn, and vaccination across the country was briefly paused while every batch was checked. About 120,000 doses of the faulty vaccine had been given. Around 40,000 children developed mild, short-lived polio illness. About 200 people, many of them children and some of them family members or neighbours who caught the virus from vaccinated children, were left with some paralysis, and about ten died. Different studies count the cases slightly differently, but this was a tragedy, and the families affected never forgot it.

Investigators found that the safety rules had not been strict enough. Tiny clumps of virus could be protected from the formaldehyde, and the tests used to check each batch were not sensitive enough to find small amounts of surviving virus. The government laboratory that was supposed to oversee vaccine makers had trusted the companies' reports too much. Several senior officials lost their jobs or resigned, including the head of the US National Institutes of Health.

The Cutter incident changed vaccine safety forever. The government created much stricter rules for how vaccines are made, filtered, tested and inspected, and set up a stronger system for overseeing them. A court case, Gottsdanker v. Cutter Laboratories, found that a company could be held responsible for harm caused by its vaccine even if it had not been careless, which shaped laws about vaccines for decades. In a way, the strict safety testing described in part 12 of this story grew partly out of this painful lesson. With the new rules in place, vaccination started again, and the Salk vaccine went on to protect many millions of children.

The results were dramatic. In 1952 the United States had reported almost 58,000 polio cases. By 1957, after two years of Salk vaccine, there were about 5,600. Parents who had dreaded every summer began, slowly, to relax.

sections.heading: Albert Sabin's Sugar Cubes
paragraphs: Albert Sabin did not think the Salk vaccine was good enough. Sabin was born Abram Saperstejn in 1906 in Białystok, then part of the Russian Empire and now in Poland. His Jewish family emigrated to the United States in 1921 to escape poverty and persecution, and he grew up to study medicine and become an expert on viruses. From 1939 he worked at the Children's Hospital in Cincinnati, Ohio, where he spent about thirty years.

Sabin had made an important discovery by studying people who had died of polio. He showed that the virus multiplies first in the gut, and only later, in a few people, reaches the nervous system. So, he reasoned, the best vaccine would build protection right where the virus first takes hold: in the gut. An injected, killed vaccine like Salk's taught the blood to make antibodies, which stopped the virus reaching the nerves, but it did not stop the virus from multiplying in the intestines and being passed on to others nearly as well.

Sabin's idea was a live attenuated vaccine. Attenuated means weakened. He grew the three types of poliovirus over and over again in cells, at lower-than-normal temperatures and under other conditions, picking out strains that had changed so they could still multiply in the gut but had almost lost the ability to damage nerves. A person would swallow these weakened viruses. The viruses would multiply harmlessly in the gut for a while, and the immune system would learn to fight them, both in the blood and in the lining of the intestines.

It was not the only live polio vaccine. Another scientist, Hilary Koprowski, had already given a live, weakened oral vaccine to a child in 1950, and his vaccines were used in some countries. But Sabin's strains became the ones used worldwide.

By the mid-1950s, the US already had the Salk vaccine, and most American families had received it, so it was hard to run a big trial of Sabin's vaccine there. The answer came from an unexpected place: the Soviet Union, America's great rival in the Cold War. Soviet scientists Mikhail Chumakov and Marina Voroshilova worked with Sabin, who shared his virus strains and advice on how to make the vaccine. In 1959 about ten million children in the Soviet Union received the oral vaccine, and by 1961 tens of millions more people had been given it across the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe and other countries. The results showed it was safe and very effective. At a time when the two superpowers were building nuclear weapons aimed at each other, their scientists were quietly working together against a shared enemy.

The oral vaccine had another great advantage: it was easy to give. There was no needle. A few drops of liquid were placed in the mouth, or dripped onto a sugar cube to hide the bitter taste, and children simply ate the sugar cube. Huge numbers of people could be vaccinated in one day by volunteers. In 1960 more than 78,000 schoolchildren in Cincinnati received the oral vaccine. In the US it was licensed in stages, for types 1 and 2 in 1961 and type 3 in 1962, and a combined version came a little later. On special mass vaccination days, families lined up at schools and clinics to eat their sugar cubes. Like Salk, Sabin did not make a fortune from his vaccine. He died in 1993, at the age of 86.

sections.heading: Two Vaccines, One Trade-off
paragraphs: So which vaccine was better? The honest answer is that each has strengths and weaknesses, and doctors have been weighing them for over sixty years.

The oral vaccine is cheap, easy to give without needles or trained nurses, and builds strong protection in the gut. That gut protection is what stops vaccinated people from passing on wild poliovirus, the natural, dangerous virus, so it is very good at stopping outbreaks. Weakened vaccine virus can even spread from a vaccinated child to people around them, which can quietly immunise them too.

But the oral vaccine has a rare downside. Because it contains live virus, on very rare occasions the weakened virus changes back into a form that can cause paralysis. This happens in roughly one in every 2.7 million doses. And in communities where few children are vaccinated, the weakened virus can pass from person to person for a long time, slowly changing until it can cause outbreaks of its own. These are called vaccine-derived polio outbreaks, and they are rare but real. The injected Salk-type vaccine, by contrast, contains only killed virus. It can never cause polio, though it is more expensive, needs a needle and a trained health worker, and is less good at stopping the virus spreading through the gut.

For this reason, as polio disappeared from wealthy countries, many of them switched to the injected vaccine, often called IPV, for inactivated polio vaccine. An improved, more powerful version of Salk's vaccine was licensed in the US in 1987, and by around 2000 the US was using only injected vaccine. Many countries where polio was a bigger threat continued to use the oral vaccine, often called OPV, and many now use a mix of both. Scientists have also designed a new, more stable version of the oral vaccine for type 2, called nOPV2, which is much less likely to change back into a dangerous form; it was fully approved by WHO in December 2023.

Thanks to both vaccines, polio fell away with astonishing speed. US cases dropped from about 58,000 in 1952 to just 161 in 1961, well under 1,000 a year. The last cases caused by wild poliovirus spreading naturally in the United States happened in 1979. Other wealthy countries saw the same thing. A disease that had terrified parents every summer for half a century had become rare within a decade.

Around the world, the fight went on. In 1988, when wild poliovirus was still paralysing an estimated 350,000 children a year in more than 125 countries, the World Health Organization, UNICEF, Rotary International and other partners launched the Global Polio Eradication Initiative. Since then, wild polio cases have fallen by more than 99 percent. Wild poliovirus type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015, and type 3 in 2019. Only wild type 1 is left, and it still spreads in parts of just two countries, Pakistan and Afghanistan. Polio is not yet eradicated, but it is closer than ever before. You will hear how that final push is going in part 19.

Salk and Sabin argued with each other for the rest of their lives about whose vaccine was best. Yet in the end, the world needed both of them, along with Enders, Weller and Robbins, Henrietta Lacks, Thomas Francis Jr., the scientists at Tuskegee, Mikhail Chumakov, and nearly two million Polio Pioneers. Their success raised a thrilling question. If polio could be pushed out of one country, could a disease be wiped out everywhere, from every country on Earth, forever? Scientists already had a target in mind: the oldest enemy in this whole story, smallpox.

deepDive: The 1954 Francis Field Trial is a landmark in the history of medical statistics. Its organisers faced a hard problem: paralytic polio was rare even in epidemic years, striking only a few dozen children per 100,000, so a trial had to be enormous to show a clear difference. The National Foundation originally favoured an observed-control design, vaccinating second-graders and comparing them with unvaccinated first- and third-graders. Francis and many statisticians worried this would be biased: parents who volunteered their children might differ from those who did not, and doctors who knew a child's vaccination status might diagnose borderline cases differently. The compromise was to run both designs. In the randomised, double-blind placebo areas, roughly 200,000 children received vaccine and a similar number received placebo, and paralytic polio was markedly less common in the vaccine group. The observed-control areas gave broadly similar results, but statisticians still point to the placebo arm as the more trustworthy evidence, and the trial is often taught as a classic example of why randomisation and blinding matter. The Cutter incident is debated differently. Paul Offit's 2005 history argues that the US lawsuit that followed, Gottsdanker v. Cutter Laboratories, which held a manufacturer liable without proof of negligence, helped push companies out of vaccine making and eventually led to the US National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act of 1986, which created a no-fault compensation programme. Counts of Cutter-related cases also vary between sources, from about 200 to over 250 paralytic cases including family contacts, depending on how cases were defined. The Salk-versus-Sabin debate continues in modified form today. Oral vaccine is better at blocking intestinal infection and transmission, which made it the workhorse of global eradication, but each dose carries a tiny risk of vaccine-associated paralysis, and in poorly immunised populations vaccine-derived viruses can circulate. In 2016 every country using oral vaccine switched from the three-type version to a two-type version without type 2, because wild type 2 had been eradicated and the type 2 vaccine strain was causing most vaccine-derived outbreaks. The eventual goal is to stop all oral vaccine use once wild virus is gone, relying on inactivated vaccine to protect against any lingering risk.
funFact: When Salk's polio vaccine results were announced on 12 April 1955, the date was chosen to fall exactly ten years after the death of Franklin Roosevelt, who had founded the March of Dimes to fight polio.

check.q: What was the main difference between Jonas Salk's and Albert Sabin's polio vaccines?
check.a: Salk's was an injection of killed (inactivated) virus; Sabin's was swallowed and used live, weakened virus
wrong: Salk's used live virus on a sugar cube; Sabin's was a killed-virus injection
Salk's was made from cowpox; Sabin's was made from horsepox
Both were nasal sprays, but Sabin's was given only to adults
